# The mental verbs

THIS BOOK IS A WORK IN PROGRESS. IT IS INCOMPLETE AND MAY HAVE TYPOGRAPHICAL AND OTHER ERRORS.

## Introduction

Consider the sentence:

(@) [زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}  
    [Zayd is standing.]{.trans}  

This entire sentence can be the inner sentence of a compound sentence as the direct object of the verb
[قَالَ]{.ar}.
So we can say:

(@) [قُلْتُ زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}  
    [I said, "Zayd is standing."]{.trans}  

In example () above, the verb
[قَالَ]{.ar}
does not exercise its government _within_ the inner sentence
[زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}.
Rather, the inner sentence is,
as a whole,
the (positional) direct object.
This is because the verb
[قَالَ]{.ar}
does not have a meaningful connection with the
_content_ of the inner sentence.
It is simply relating the sentence as direct speech.

In addition to a nounal sentence like
[زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar},
a verbal sentence too can be the direct object of
[قَالَ]{.ar}.
So, for example,
we can say:

(@) [قُلْتُ ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [I said, "Zayd beat."]{.trans}  

Now let's consider what happens when a
nounal sentence is made the direct object of a class of verbs
called _mental verbs_.

_Mental verbs_ are a class
of verbs that signify actions taking place within the mind.
Some examples of mental verbs are:

+ [ظَنَّ]{.ar} [to conjecture, assume]{.trans}
+ [عَلِمَ]{.ar} [to know]{.trans}
+ [حَسِبَ]{.ar} [to deem]{.trans}
+ [خَالَ]{.ar} [to imagine]{.trans}

These verbs can take a inner nounal sentence
as a direct object,
but instead of taking the entire inner sentence as one direct object,
the mental verb
exercises its government within the inner sentence
and governs the
original subject and info of the inner sentence individually
as two direct objects.
For example:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}  
    [I assumed Zayd to be standing.]{.trans}  

Note that 
[زَيْدًا]{.ar}
and
[قَائِمًا]{.ar}
are both in the a-case
because they are,
individually,
the direct objects of [ظَنَّ]{.ar}.
The verb [ظَنَّ]{.ar}
is able to break up the original
nounal sentence
[زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}
and govern its constituents individually
because it has a meaningful connection with the
content of the inner sentence.
This is because
the original subject ([زَيْد]{.ar})'s relationship with
the original info ([قَائِم]{.ar})
is only established via the meaning of the verb [ظَنَّ]{.ar}.
That is,
the sentence
in example () above
is not saying that Zayd is standing.
Rather it is saying that _I thought_ Zayd to be standing.
So Zayd's "standing-ness" is only established via my assumption of it.

The mental verb thus describes the
nature of speaker's belief
of the actuality of the
original
info
ocurring from the original subject.^[[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 4/153](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1588&part=4#p-23090-1588-2)]

So, for example,
[ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}
signifies my _assumption_ of Zayd's standing.
And
[عَلِمْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}
signifies my _knowledge_ of Zayd's standing.


## The lean of the mental verb sentence

The basic nounal sentence consists of a subject and a info.
For example:

(@) [زَيْدٌ أَخُوكَ]{.ar}  
    [Zayd is your brother.]{.trans}  

In example () above,
[زَيْدٌ]{.ar}
is the subject
and
[أَخُوكَ]{.ar}
is its info.
Both are in the u-case because it is a basic nounal sentence.
In terms of its lean,
[زَيْدٌ]{.ar}
is the leaned-against element
and
[أَخُوكَ]{.ar}
is the leaning element.
(Technically, the leaning element is [أَخ]{.ar}. And it in turn is a annexe to the annexed-to [كَ]{.ar}.
But loosely speaking, we can say that the leaning element is the bundled [أَخُوكَ]{.ar}.)
With the leaned-against element and the leaning element in place, the sentence is leaned.

Now consider the following sentence:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا أَخَاكَ]{.ar}
    [Peled, _Sentence types_ 188]{.citex}  
    [I thought Zayd to be your brother.]{.trans}  

In example () above,
the verb [ظَنَّ]{.ar}
takes the subject and info of example (),
and makes them into direct objects.
The verb [ظَنَّ]{.ar}
requires a doer (as usual),
which is the pronoun [تُ]{.ar} [I]{.trans}.
And it also requires two direct objects:
[زَيْدًا]{.ar}
is the first direct object
and
[أَخَاكَ]{.ar}
is the second direct object.

This sentence is peculiar in its lean.
This is because the indispensable elements are the two direct objects.
[زَيْدًا]{.ar}
is the leaned-against element
and
[أَخَاكَ]{.ar}
is the leaning element.^[[[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 433](https://archive.org/details/0969pdf_201912/page/n432/mode/1up)]
The sentence is only leaned when both direct objects are in place.
The sentence may still be categorized as a verbal sentence.
However, unlike normal verbal sentences,
the verb [ظَنَّ]{.ar} and its doer are not the indispensable elements of the sentence.
Rather [ظَنَّ]{.ar} is the foundational government.
Figure () depicts the government of example ().

Parallels of the lean of the [ظَنَّ]{.ar} sentence
may be found in the [كَانَ]{.ar} and [إِنَّ]{.ar} sentences:

(@) [كَانَ زَيْدٌ أَخَاكَ]{.ar}
    [Peled, _Sentence types_ 188]{.citex}  
    [Zayd was your brother.]{.trans}  
    ([زَيْدٌ]{.ar}, the doer/subject, is the leaned-against element.
    [أَخَاكَ]{.ar}, the direct object/info, is the leaning element.
    [كَانَ]{.ar} is the foundational government.)


(@) [إِنَّ زَيْدًا أَخُوكَ]{.ar}
    [Peled, _Sentence types_ 188]{.citex}  
    [Indeed Zayd is your brother.]{.trans}  
    ([زَيْدًا]{.ar}, the subject, is the leaned-against element.
    [أَخُوكَ]{.ar}, the info, is the leaning element.
    [إِنَّ]{.ar} is the foundational government.)

## The mental verbs as passive verbs

When mental verbs are used in the passive voice,
the first direct object
(the one which is the subject in the basic nounal sentence)
is made the deputy doer in the u-case.
And the second direct object
(the one which is the info in the basic nounal sentence)
remains a direct object in the a-case.
So, example () above, becomes in the passive voice:

(@) [ظُنَّ زَيْدٌ أَخَاكَ]{.ar}  
    [Zayd was thought to be your brother.]{.trans}

Similarly,

(@) [زَيْدٌ مَظْنُونٌ شُجَاعًا]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/52D]{.citex}  
    [Zayd is thought to be brave.]{.trans}  


## [أَنَّ]{.ar} and [أَنْ]{.ar} with mental verbs

Consider again the sentence:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}  
    [I assumed Zayd to be standing.]{.trans}  

Literally
[زَيْدًا]{.ar}
and
[قَائِمًا]{.ar}
are both,
individually,
the direct objects of [ظَنَّ]{.ar}.
However,
in terms of meaning,
the [taqdIr]{.trn2} of the sentence is:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ قِيَامَ زَيْدٍ]{.ar}  
    [I assumed Zayd to be standing.]{.trans}  

That is,
in the [taqdIr]{.trn2} of the sentence,
[ظَنَّ]{.ar} has one direct object which is the
[maSdar]{.trn2}
([قِيَام]{.ar})
of the second direct object
([قَائِم]{.ar})
annexed to the first direct object
([زَيْد]{.ar}).

We have seen
[maSdar]{.trn2}s as a [taqdIr]{.trn2} before
in the analysis of
[أَنَّ]{.ar} and [أَنْ]{.ar}.
And this similarity allows
[أَنَّ]{.ar} and [أَنْ]{.ar} (with their clauses)
to optionally occur as the direct object of mental verbs.^[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar}; [النحو الوافي]{.ar} 2/43]
So instead of saying
[ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar},
we can instead say:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ [أَنَّ]{.eghl} زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ]{.ar}  
    [I assumed [that]{.eghl} Zayd is standing.]{.trans}  

or:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ [أَنْ]{.eghl} يَقُومَ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}  
    [I assumed [that]{.eghl} Zayd would stand.]{.trans}  

Now the [أَنَّ]{.ar} and [أَنْ]{.ar} clauses, respectively,
are, formally,
the single direct object of [ظَنَّ]{.ar}.
This substitution of the two direct objects
of mental verbs
can be considered a form of _suspension_,^[[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للعثيمين]{.ar} 28/3](https://shamela.ws/book/36954/273); [[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للحازمي]{.ar} 43/2](https://shamela.ws/book/36130/789)]
but is really more basic than it.
We will study suspension in @sec-ta3leeq below, if Allāh wills.

In terms of meaning,
example () above is more assertive than
the original example ().
Whereas,
example () is less assertive and more doubtful than
the original example ().

Here is another example of substituting the
direct objects of a mental verb
with an [أَنَّ]{.ar} clause:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}  
    [I knew Zayd to be standing.]{.trans}  

(@) [عَلِمْتُ [أَنَّ]{.eghl} زَيْدًا قَائِمٌ]{.ar}  
    [I knew [that]{.eghl} Zayd is standing.]{.trans}  

In this case, we will only use [أَنَّ]{.ar}
and not [أَنْ]{.ar}
because,
as we learned in section\ (),
only [أَنَّ]{.ar} is used in cases of certainty,
which is what the verb [عَلِمَ]{.ar} implies.

In examples () and (),
it was easy to come up with a [maSdar]{.trn2}i equivalence of the
two direct objects of the mental verbs.
This is because the second direct object
([قَائِم]{.ar})
was a deverbal noun.
But what if the
the second direct object was a primitive noun?
For example:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ أَخَاكَ زَيْدًا]{.ar}
    [[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 3/152](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1587&part=4#p-23090-1587-2)]{.citex}  
    [I knew your brother to be Zayd.]{.trans}  

In this case we can manufacture a [maSdar]{.trn2} from the primitive noun,
and still retain the [taqdIr]{.trn2}, thus:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ [زَيْدِيَّةَ]{.eghl} أَخِيكَ]{.ar}
    [[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 3/152](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1587&part=4#p-23090-1587-2)]{.citex}  
    [I knew the [Zayd-ness]{.eghl} of your brother.]{.trans}  

And using this [maSdar]{.trn2}i equivalence,
we can substitute it with [أَنَّ]{.ar}, thus:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ [أَنَّ]{.eghl} أَخَاكَ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}  
    [I knew [that]{.eghl} your brother is Zayd.]{.trans}

## The verbs that comprise the mental verbs

### [ظَنَّ]{.ar}

[ظَنَّ يَظُنُّ]{.ar}
is the typical mental verb.
Its basic meaning is 
[to conjecture]{.trans}
or
[to assume]{.trans}.
But it (and the mental verbs in general)
can often be translated as
[to think]{.trans}.

[ظَنَّ]{.ar}
can be used in a range of circumstances from
situations
where its doer believes something to be certain,
to cases where he is doubtful.
Here are some examples:

(@) [وَإِنِّی لَأَظُنُّكَ یَـٰفِرۡعَوۡنُ مَثۡبُورࣰا]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الإسراء]{.ar} 17:102](https://quran.com/17/102) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/331]{.citex}  
    [and indeed I think, O Pharaoh, that you are destroyed.]{.trans}  

(@) [قُلۡتُم مَّا نَدۡرِی مَا ٱلسَّاعَةُ إِن نَّظُنُّ إِلَّا ظَنࣰّا وَمَا نَحۡنُ بِمُسۡتَیۡقِنِینَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الجاثية]{.ar} 45:32](https://quran.com/45/32) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/331]{.citex}  
    [you said, 'We know not what is the Hour. We assume only assumption, and we are not convinced.']{.trans}  

(@) [ظَنَنْتُكَ إِنْ شَبَّتْ لَظَى الْحَرْبِ صَالِيًا]{.ar}
    [cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/331]{.citex}  
    [I thought you, if the blaze of war is kindled, to be entering (therein)]{.trans}  

[ظَنَّ]{.ar} following examples is interpreted to have certainty in its meaning:

(@) [قَالَ ٱلَّذِینَ یَظُنُّونَ أَنَّهُم مُّلَـٰقُوا۟ ٱللَّهِ كَم مِّن فِئَةࣲ قَلِیلَةٍ غَلَبَتۡ فِئَةࣰ كَثِیرَةَۢ بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِۗ وَٱللَّهُ مَعَ ٱلصَّـٰبِرِینَ]{.quran}^[See [[تفسير ابن عثيمين]{.ar} for [سورة البقرة]{.ar} 2:249](https://tafsir.app/ibn-uthaymeen/2/249)]
    [[[سورة البقرة]{.ar} 2:249](https://quran.com/2/249) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/332]{.citex}  
    [But those who were certain that they would meet Allāh said, "How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allāh. And Allāh is with the patient."]{.trans}

(@) [إِنِّی ظَنَنتُ أَنِّی مُلَـٰقٍ حِسَابِیَهۡ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الحاقة]{.ar} 69:20](https://quran.com/69/20) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/332]{.citex}  
    [Indeed, I was certain that I would be meeting my account."]{.trans}  

(@) [وَرَءَا ٱلۡمُجۡرِمُونَ ٱلنَّارَ فَظَنُّوۤا۟ أَنَّهُم مُّوَاقِعُوهَا وَلَمۡ یَجِدُوا۟ عَنۡهَا مَصۡرِفࣰا]{.quran}^[See [[تفسير ابن عثيمين]{.ar} for [سورة الكهف]{.ar} 18:53](https://tafsir.app/ibn-uthaymeen/18/53)]
    [[[سورة الكهف]{.ar} 18:53](https://quran.com/18/53) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/332]{.citex}  
    [And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are to fall therein. And they will not find from it a way elsewhere.]{.trans}  

[ظَنَّ]{.ar} can be used with both [أَنَّ]{.ar}
(as above)
and the a-case-izing [أَنْ]{.ar}.
Here is an example with the a-case-izing [أَنْ]{.ar}:

(@) [تَظُنُّ [أَن]{.eghl} یُفۡعَلَ بِهَا فَاقِرَةࣱ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة القيامة]{.ar} 75:25](https://quran.com/75/25)]{.citex}

Even so, example () above is interpreted to have certitude,
or at least a preponderance of belief,
in its
meaning.^[[[البحر المحيط لأبي حيان]{.ar} for [سورة القيامة]{.ar} 75:25](https://tafsir.app/albahr-almuheet/75/25)]

The lightened [أَنْ]{.ar} can also be used.
For example:

(@) [وَظَنُّوۤا۟ [أَن]{.eghl} لَّا مَلۡجَأَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّاۤ إِلَیۡهِ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة التوبة]{.ar} 9:118](https://quran.com/9/118)]{.citex}  

[أَنْ]{.ar} in example () above is interpreted to be
the lightened [أَنْ]{.ar}.^[[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة التوبة]{.ar} 9:118](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/9/118)]

Sometimes [ظَنَّ]{.ar}
can have a specialized meaning
[to suspect]{.trans}.
In this case, it no longer needs two direct objects,
and will take only one direct object.
For example:

(@) [ظَنَّ القَاضِي فُلَانًا]{.ar}
    [[النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/331]{.citex}  
    [The judge suspected so-and-so.]{.trans}  

(@) [عُدِمَ لِي مَالٌ فَظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §442 2/150](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=211)]{.citex}  
    [Some property of mine was missing so I suspected Zayd.]{.trans}  

### [عَلِمَ]{.ar}

[عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ]{.ar}
means
[to know]{.trans}.
Here are some examples of its usage:

(@) [عَلِمْتُكَ الْبَاذِلَ الْمَعْرُوفَ]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/49B]{.citex}  
    [I have known you to be liberal in the exercise of bounty.]{.trans}  

(@) [فَإِنۡ [عَلِمۡتُمُوهُنَّ مُؤۡمِنَـٰتࣲ]{.eghl} فَلَا تَرۡجِعُوهُنَّ إِلَى ٱلۡكُفَّارِۖ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الممتحنة]{.ar} 60:10](https://quran.com/60/10) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/325]{.citex}  
    [And if [you know them to be believers]{.eghl}, then do not return them to the disbelievers;]{.trans}  

(@) [عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، وَالْحَسَنِ بْنِ عَلِيٍّ ، مَرَّتْ بِهِمَا جَنَازَةٌ فَقَامَ أَحَدُهُمَا وَقَعَدَ الآخَرُ فَقَالَ الَّذِي قَامَ أَمَا وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ [عَلِمْتُ أَنَّ]{.eghl} رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَدْ قَامَ قَالَ لَهُ الَّذِي جَلَسَ لَقَدْ [عَلِمْتُ أَنَّ]{.eghl} رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَدْ جَلَسَ]{.ar}
    [[[سنن النسائي]{.ar} :1926](https://sunnah.com/nasai:1926)]{.citex}  
    [[It was narrated] from Ibn [#eabbAs]{.trn2} and [al-#Hasan ibn #ealiyy]{.trn2}: A funeral passed by them and one of them stood and the other [stayed] seated. The one who stood up said, "By Allāh, [I know that]{.eghl} the Messenger of Allāh [ﷺ]{.areng} had stood up." The one who [stayed] seated said to him, "Indeed [I know that]{.eghl} the Messenger of Allāh [ﷺ]{.areng} had [stayed] seated."]{.trans}

(@) [إِنَّ رَبَّكَ [یَعۡلَمُ أَنَّكَ تَقُومُ]{.eghl} أَدۡنَىٰ مِن ثُلُثَیِ ٱلَّیۡلِ وَنِصۡفَهُۥ وَثُلُثَهُۥ وَطَاۤىِٕفَةࣱ مِّنَ ٱلَّذِینَ مَعَكَۚ وَٱللَّهُ یُقَدِّرُ ٱلَّیۡلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَۚ [عَلِمَ أَن لَّن تُحۡصُوهُ]{.eghl} فَتَابَ عَلَیۡكُمۡۖ فَٱقۡرَءُوا۟ مَا تَیَسَّرَ مِنَ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانِۚ [عَلِمَ أَن سَیَكُونُ مِنكُم مَّرۡضَىٰ]{.eghl} وَءَاخَرُونَ یَضۡرِبُونَ فِی ٱلۡأَرۡضِ یَبۡتَغُونَ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ وَءَاخَرُونَ یُقَـٰتِلُونَ فِی سَبِیلِ ٱللَّهِۖ فَٱقۡرَءُوا۟ مَا تَیَسَّرَ مِنۡهُۚ وَأَقِیمُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُوا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَأَقۡرِضُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ قَرۡضًا حَسَنࣰاۚ وَمَا تُقَدِّمُوا۟ لِأَنفُسِكُم مِّنۡ خَیۡرࣲ تَجِدُوهُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ هُوَ خَیۡرࣰا وَأَعۡظَمَ أَجۡرࣰاۚ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِیمُۢ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة المزمل]{.ar} 73:20](https://quran.com/73/20)]{.citex}  
    [Indeed, [your Lord knows, [O Muḥammad], that you stand [in prayer]]{.eghl} almost two thirds of the night or half of it or a third of it, and [so do] a group of those with you. And Allāh determines [the extent of] the night and the day. [He has known that you [Muslims] will not be able to do it]{.eghl} and has turned to you in forgiveness, so recite what is easy [for you] of the Qur’ān. [He has known that there will be among you those who are ill]{.eghl} and others traveling throughout the land seeking [something] of the bounty of Allāh and others fighting for the cause of Allāh. So recite what is easy from it and establish prayer and give zakāh and loan Allāh a goodly loan. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves - you will find it with Allāh. It is better and greater in reward. And seek forgiveness of Allāh. Indeed, Allāh is Forgiving and Merciful.]{.trans}  
    ([أَنْ]{.ar} in [أَنْ لَنْ]{.ar} and [أَنْ سيكونُ]{.ar} is the lightened [أَنْ]{.ar},^[[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة المزمل]{.ar} 73:20](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/73/20)] whose subject is a deleted state-of-affairs pronoun.^[[[إعراب القرآن للدرويش]{.ar} for [سورة المزمل]{.ar} 73:20](https://tafsir.app/iraab-aldarweesh/73/20)])

is special in that it can take only one direct object,
even without [أَنَّ]{.ar},

For example:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ زَيْدًا]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية (جامعة الإمام محمد)]{.ar} 2/988]{.citex}  
    [I knew Zayd.]{.trans}  

(@) [عَلِمْتُ خُرُوجَ زَيْدٍ]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية (جامعة الإمام محمد)]{.ar} 2/988]{.citex}  
    [I knew Zayd's going out.]{.trans}

### [رَأَى]{.ar}

[رَأَى يَرَى]{.ar},
as a sensory verb,
means
[to see]{.trans} with the eye.
As such, it will typically take
one direct object.
For example:

(@) [رَأَيْتُهُ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §442 2/150](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=211)]{.citex}  
    [I saw him]{.trans}  

When [رَأَىٰ]{.ar} has this sensory meaning,
then there may be a second a-case (indefinite) governee as a [HAl]{.trn2}.^[[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 445]
For example:

(@) [رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا ضَاحِكًا]{.ar}
    [[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 445]{.citex}  
    [I saw Zayd laughing.]{.trans}  

[رَأَىٰ]{.ar}
can also mean
[to hold (an opinion)]{.trans}.
In this case as well, it will take one direct object.
For example:

(@) [رَأَىٰ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ حِلَّ كَذَا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §442 2/150](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=211)]{.citex}  
    [[#abU #HanIfah]{.trn2} held (the opinion of) the lawfulness of such a thing.]{.trans}

As a mental verb,
[رَأَى]{.ar}
means
[to regard]{.trans} in the mind.
It may still be translated as
[to see]{.trans},
but this "seeing" is with the mind.
Now
[رَأَى]{.ar}
will take take two direct objects.

Here are some examples of
[رَأَى]{.ar}:

(@) [رَأَيْتُ اللهَ أَكْبَرَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مُحَاوَلَةً وَأَكْثَرُهُمْ جُنُودًا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §440 2/134](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=195)]{.citex}  
    [I regarded Allāh as the greatest of eveything in resource, and the most numerous of them in hosts.]{.trans}  

(@) [إِنَّهُمۡ یَرَوۡنَهُۥ بَعِیدࣰا۝ وَنَرَىٰهُ قَرِیبࣰا۝]{.quran}
    [[[سورة المعارج]{.ar} 70:6–7](https://quran.com/70/6-7)]{.citex}  
    [Indeed, they see it [as] distant, But We see it [as] near.]{.trans}

Even when
[رَأَى]{.ar}
contains the meaning of a sensory verb,
it can still take two direct objects
when the mind takes what it sees
and regards it to be something.^[See [البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 447; [[شرح التسهيل لابن مالك]{.ar} 2/327](https://shamela.ws/book/13257/723); [[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة يوسف]{.ar} 12:4](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/12/4); [[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 4/151](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1586&part=4#p-23090-1586-2)]
For example:

(@) [يَا مَعْشَرَ النِّسَاءِ تَصَدَّقْنَ وَأَكْثِرْنَ فَإِنِّي [رَأَيْتُكُنَّ أَكْثَرَ أَهْلِ النَّارِ]{.eghl} لِكَثْرَةِ اللَّعْنِ وَكُفْرِ الْعَشِيرِ]{.ar}
    [[[مسند أحمد]{.ar} :5343](https://hadithunlocked.com/ahmad:5343) cited by [البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 447 footnote 1]{.citex}  
    [O women, give charity and do a lot of it, for indeed [I saw you to be the majority of the people of the Fire]{.eghl}, because of much cursing [on your part] and being ungrateful to the husband.]{.trans}  

(@) [رَأَیۡتُهُمۡ لِی سَـٰجِدِینَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة يوسف]{.ar} 12:4](https://quran.com/12/4) cited by [[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 4/151](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1586&part=4#p-23090-1586-2)]{.citex}  
    [I saw them prostrating to me.]{.trans}  

### [حَسِبَ]{.ar}

[حَسِبَ يَحْسَِبُ]{.ar}
means [to deem]{.trans}.
As with [ظَنَّ]{.ar},
it can be translated with the verb [think]{.trans}.
Here are some examples:

(@) [حَسِبْتُ التُّقَىٰ وَالْجُودَ خَيْرَ تِجَارَةٍ رَبَاحًا]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/49C]{.citex}  
    [I deemed piety and generosity the best merchandise, in terms of profit.]{.trans}  

(@) [وَلَا تَحۡسَبَنَّ ٱلَّذِینَ قُتِلُوا۟ فِی سَبِیلِ ٱللَّهِ أَمۡوَ ٰ⁠تَۢاۚ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة آل عمران]{.ar} 3:169](https://quran.com/3/169) cited by Wright 2/49C]{.citex}  
    [And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allāh as dead.]{.trans}  

(@) [صَنَعْنَا لِرَسُولِ اللهِ ﷺ فَخَّارَةً ، فَأَتَيْتُهُ بِهَا ، فَوَضَعْتُهَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ ، فَاطَّلَعَ فِيهَا ، فَقَالَ : [حَسِبْتُهُ لَحْمًا]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[[مسند أحمد]{.ar} :14581](https://hadithunlocked.com/ahmad:14581)]{.citex}  
    [We made a (clay) pot (of food) for the Messenger of Allāh [ﷺ]{.areng} and I brought it to him. He peered into it and said, "[I thought it was meat.]{.eghl}"]{.trans}  

(@) [أَحَسِبَ ٱلنَّاسُ [أَن یُتۡرَكُوۤا۟]{.eghl} أَن یَقُولُوۤا۟ ءَامَنَّا وَهُمۡ لَا یُفۡتَنُونَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة العنكبوت]{.ar} 29:2](https://quran.com/29/2) cited by [[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للحازمي]{.ar} 43/2](https://shamela.ws/book/36130/789)]{.citex}  
    [Do the people think [that they will be left]{.eghl} to say, "We believe" and they will not be tried?]{.trans}  
    (The [maSdar]{.trn2} from [أَنْ يُتْرَكُوا]{.ar} fulfils the role of the two direct objects.^[[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للحازمي]{.ar} 43/2](https://shamela.ws/book/36130/789); [[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة العنكبوت]{.ar} 29:2](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/29/2)])

### [وَجَدَ]{.ar}

[وَجَدَ يَجِدُ]{.ar}
is also a sensory verb which means [to find]{.trans}.
When it is used to mean that the mind has found something to be another thing,
then it is used as a mental verb
and can take two direct objects.
Examples:

(@) [وَإِن وَجَدۡنَاۤ أَكۡثَرَهُمۡ لَفَـٰسِقِینَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأعراف]{.ar} 7:102](https://quran.com/7/102) cited by [[شرح ابن عقيل على الألفية]{.ar} 2/31](https://shamela.ws/book/9904/418)]{.citex}  
    [but indeed, We found most of them defiantly disobedient.]{.trans}  
    ([أَكْثَرَهُمْ]{.ar} and [لَفَاسِقِينَ]{.ar} are both analyzed to be direct objects.)  


(@) [كُنَّا مَعْشَرُ قُرَيْشٍ قَوْمًا نَغْلِبُ النِّسَاءَ فَلَمَّا قَدِمْنَا الْمَدِينَةَ [وَجَدْنَاهُمْ قَوْمًا]{.eghl} تَغْلِبُهُمْ نِسَاؤُهُمْ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح ابن حبان]{.ar} :4268a](https://hadithunlocked.com/ibnhibban:4268a)]{.citex}  
    [We, the people of [#qurayc]{.trn2}, were a people who were dominant over the women. But when we came to [al-#madInah]{.trn2}, [we found them to be a people]{.eghl} whose women dominated them.]{.trans}  

As with
[رَأَى]{.ar},
when
[وَجَدَ]{.ar}
is used merely as a sensory verb,
then it will take only one direct object.
A second a-case noun with it will then be construed as a [HAl]{.trn2}.^[Wright 2/50C]
For example:

(@) [وَجَدْتُهُ [مَرِيضًا]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/50C]{.citex}  
    [I found him [sick]{.eghl}.]{.trans}  
    ([مَرِيضًا]{.ar} is a [HAl]{.trn2}.)

Similarly:

(@) [أَلَمۡ یَجِدۡكَ [یَتِیمࣰا]{.eghl} فَـَٔاوَىٰ۝ وَوَجَدَكَ [ضَاۤلࣰّا]{.eghl} فَهَدَىٰ۝ وَوَجَدَكَ [عَاۤىِٕلࣰا]{.eghl} فَأَغۡنَىٰ۝]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الضحى]{.ar} 93:6–8](https://quran.com/93/6-8)]{.citex}  
    [Did He not find you [an orphan]{.eghl} and give [you] refuge?  And He found you [lost]{.eghl} and guided [you], And He found you [poor]{.eghl} and made [you] self-sufficient.]{.trans}  
    ([يَتِيمًا]{.ar}, [ضَالًّا]{.ar}, and [عَائِلًا]{.ar} are analyzed as [HAl]{.trn2}s.^[[[تفسير ابن عاشور]{.ar} for [سورة الضحى]{.ar} 93:6](https://tafsir.app/ibn-aashoor/93/6)] Although, a direct object interpretation for at least one of them also seems to be possible.^[[[إعراب القرآن للدرويش]{.ar} for [سورة الضحى]{.ar} 93:6](https://tafsir.app/iraab-aldarweesh/93/6)])  

### [خَالَ]{.ar}

[خَالَ يَخَالُ خِلْتُ]{.ar}
means [to imagine or fancy (something)]{.trans}.
It too is often translated as [to think]{.trans}.
[خَالَ]{.ar} is irregular in that its 
speaker participant singular for the
[pc]{.smallcaps} verb
([I imagine]{.trans})
is more commonly
[[إِ]{.eghl}خَالُ]{.ar}
[[Ei]{.eghl}xAlu]{.trn}
instead of
[[أَ]{.eghl}خَالُ]{.ar}
[[Ea]{.eghl}xAlu]{.trn}.
For example,

(@) [إِخَالُ زَيْدًا أَخَاكَ]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/49C]{.citex}  
    [I imagine Zayd to be your brother.]{.trans}  

Here are some examples of [خَالَ]{.ar} as a mental verb:

(@) [فَأُتِيَ بِكُرْسِيٍّ خِلْتُ قَوَائِمَهُ حَدِيدًا]{.ar}
    [[[سنن النسائي]{.ar} :5377](https://sunnah.com/nasai:5377)]{.citex}
    [Then he was brought a chair, whose legs I imagined to be of iron.]{.trans}  

(@) [مَا إِخَالُ أَحَدًا يَعْقِلُ يَرْمِي حَتَّى تَطْلُعَ الشَّمْسُ]{.ar}
    [[[مسند أحمد]{.ar} :2082](https://hadithunlocked.com/ahmad:2082)]{.citex}  
    [I don't imagine anyone of sense to stone until the sun rises.]{.trans}  

    (The first direct object is [أَحَدًا]{.ar}. And the second direct object is the verbal sentence [يَرْمِي]{.ar}.)  

### [زَعَمَ]{.ar}

[زَعَمَ]{.ar} means [to claim]{.trans}.


### [دَرَى]{.ar}

Usually used only with [أَنَّ]{.ar}.^[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} claims it is only used with [أَنَّ]{.ar}]
Examples:

Rarely, it can take two direct objects directly.
For example:

[Howell 2/135]{.citex}

### [تَعَلَّمْ]{.ar}

rigid

Usually used only with [أَنَّ]{.ar}.^[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} claims it is only used with [أَنَّ]{.ar}]
Examples:

Rarely, it can take two direct objects directly.
For example:

[Howell 2/135]{.citex}

### [هَبْ]{.ar}

rigid

### [سَمِعَ]{.ar}

[سَمِعَ]{.ar}
is, by default, a sensory verb
that means
[to hear]{.trans}.
And,
as such,
it takes one direct object.
For example:

(@) [سَمِعْتُ زَيْدًا]{.ar}  
    [I heard Zayd.]{.trans}

(@) [سَمِعْتُ صَوْتًا]{.ar}  
    [I heard a sound.]{.trans}

But,
as a special case,
[سَمِعَ]{.ar}
can take two direct objects
when the doer
hears someone to be doing something.
For example:

(@) [سَمِعْتُ زَيْدٌ قَارِئًا]{.ar}
    [[[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 446](https://archive.org/details/0969pdf_201912/page/n445/mode/1up)]{.citex}  
    [I heard Zayd reading.]{.trans}  
    (The second direct object is the noun [قَارِئًا]{.ar}.)  

(@) [سَمِعْتُ زَيْدٌ يَقْرَأُ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/165](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=226)]{.citex}  
    [I heard Zayd reading.]{.trans}  
    (The second direct object is the verbal sentence [يَقْرَأُ]{.ar}.)  

In these examples,
[قَارِئًا]{.ar}
and
[يَقْرَأُ]{.ar}
are not considered a [HAl]{.trn2}
(as [ضَاحِكًا]{.ar} was considered a [HAl]{.trn2}
in example () [رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا ضَاحِكًا]{.ar}
[I saw Zayd laughing.]{.trans}).
This is because the sentence,
in this context, would not be leaned if you did not add
the second direct object.
That is, if, in this context, you said
[سَمِعْتُ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}
and stopped,
the listener would be left wondering, "You heard Zayd doing what?"
So a second direct object has to be added which gives the action that Zayd was doing which produced a sound.^[[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة الأنبياء]{.ar} 21:60](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/21/60)]
Similarly,

(@) [قَالُوا۟ [سَمِعۡنَا فَتࣰى یَذۡكُرُهُمۡ]{.eghl} یُقَالُ لَهُۥۤ إِبۡرَ ٰ⁠هِیمُ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأنبياء]{.ar} 21:60](https://quran.com/21/60)]{.citex}  
    [They said, "[We heard a young man mention them]{.eghl} who is called Abraham."]{.trans}  
    ([يَذْكُرُهُمْ]{.ar} is analyzed to be the second direct object of [سَمِعَ]{.ar}.^[[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة الأنبياء]{.ar} 21:60](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/21/60)])

## The second direct object can be a sentence or phrase

Because mental verbs govern
what was originally a subject-info sentence,
the first direct object may be anything which is allowed to be a subject,
and
the second direct object may be anything which is allowed to be a info.
Thus, the second direct object
may be a complete sentence in the positional a-case,
or an adverbial or prepositional phrase.^[[[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 443](https://archive.org/details/0969pdf_201912/page/n441/mode/2up)]

Here are some examples
where the second direct object is a complete sentence:

(@) [[مَا عَلِمْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم نَكَحَ]{.eghl} شَيْئًا مِنْ نِسَائِهِ وَلاَ أَنْكَحَ شَيْئًا مِنْ بَنَاتِهِ عَلَى أَكْثَرَ مِنْ ثِنْتَىْ عَشْرَةَ أُوقِيَّةً]{.ar}
    [[[جامع الترمذي]{.ar} :1114b](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:1114b)]{.citex}  
    [[I did not know the Messenger of Allāh [ﷺ]{.areng} to marry]{.eghl} any of his women, nor to give any of his daughters in marriage, for more than twelve [#Uqiyah]{.trn2}s.]{.trans}  
    (First direct object is [رَسُول الله]{.ar} [the Messenger of Allāh]{.trans}, second direct object is [نَكَحَ]{.ar} [he married]{.trans}.)

(@) [[مَا عَلِمْتُهُ صَامَ]{.eghl} شَهْرًا كُلَّهُ إِلاَّ رَمَضَانَ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :1156b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1156b)]{.citex}  
    [[I did not know him to fast]{.eghl} any complete month except [#ramaDAn]{.trn2}.]{.trans}  
    (First direct object is [هُ]{.ar} [him]{.trans}, second direct object is [صَامَ]{.ar} [he fasted]{.trans}.)

(@) [[ظَنَنْتُهُ يَدْعُو]{.eghl} فِي الِاسْتِسْقَاءِ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح ابن خزيمة]{.ar} :1595](https://hadithunlocked.com/ibnkhuzaymah:1595)]{.citex}
    [[I thought him to be supplicating]{.eghl} in the rain prayer.]{.trans}  
    (First direct object is [هُ]{.ar} [him]{.trans}, second direct object is [يَدْعُو]{.ar} [supplicating]{.trans}.)

Here is an example
where the second direct object is a prepositional phrase:

(@) [قَالَ أَمَا وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ ذَلِكَ لِتَغَيُّرِ ثَائِرَةٍ كَانَتْ مِنِّي إِلَيْهِمْ وَلَكِنِّي [أَرَاهُمْ عَلَى ضَلَالَةٍ]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[[مستدرك الحاكم]{.ar} :4956](https://hadithunlocked.com/hakim:4956)]{.citex}  
    [He said, "By Allāh, indeed that is because of a change in a matter between me and them, but [I think them to be on misguidance]{.eghl}."]{.trans}  
    (First direct object is [هُمْ]{.ar} [them]{.trans}, second direct object is [عَلَى ضَلَالٍ]{.ar} [on misguidance]{.trans}.)

## The first direct object may be a state-of-affairs pronoun

Just like the second direct object may be a complete sentence,
similarly,
the first direct object may be a state-of-affairs pronoun
because a state-of-affairs pronoun can regularly be the subject of a nounal sentence.
So we can say:

(@) [حَسِبْتُ يَقُولُ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}
    [[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 3/152](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1587&part=4#p-23090-1587-2)]{.citex}  
    [I deemed [the state-of-affairs to be] Zayd is saying.]{.trans}

In example () above,
the first direct object of [حَسِبَ]{.ar}
is a deleted state-of-affairs pronoun,
as if to say:
[حَسِبْتُهُ يَقُولُ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}.^[[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 3/152](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1587&part=4#p-23090-1587-2)]

However, such usage will be rare.^[footnote]

## Mental verbs with only one direct object

So far we have focused on
mental verbs
that take two direct objects.
There are other
mental verbs
that take only one direct object,
or no direct object.
They are not so much the subject of this chapter,
except that they can undertake a phenomenon called
_suspension_ that we will study in @sec-ta3leeq below.
In any case, we give examples of some of these verbs:

[Examples of [عَرَفَ، تَفَكَّرَ]{.ar}]


Some of the mental verbs that can take two direct objects,
while keeping their meaning as
mental verbs,
can take only one direct object.
[عَلِمَ]{.ar}
is the prime example of this variation.
For example,
we may say:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ زَيْدًا]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية (جامعة الإمام محمد)]{.ar} 2/988]{.citex}  
    [I knew Zayd.]{.trans}  

(@) [عَلِمْتُ خُرُوجَ زَيْدٍ]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية (جامعة الإمام محمد)]{.ar} 2/988]{.citex}  
    [I knew Zayd's going out.]{.trans}  

Similarly:

(@) [وَٱللَّهُ أَخۡرَجَكُم مِّنۢ بُطُونِ أُمَّهَـٰتِكُمۡ [لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ شَیۡـࣰٔا]{.eghl}]{.quran}
    [[[سورة النحل]{.ar} 16:78](https://quran.com/16/78) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/236]{.citex}  
    [And Allāh has extracted you from the wombs of your mothers [not knowing a thing]{.eghl}]{.trans}  

(@) [لَقَدْ [عَلِمْتُ النَّظَائِرَ]{.eghl} الَّتِي كَانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقْرَأُ بِهِنَّ سُورَتَيْنِ فِي رَكْعَةٍ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :822e](https://sunnah.com/muslim:822e)]{.citex}  
    [[I know the manners]{.eghl} in which the Messenger of Allāh [ﷺ]{.areng} recited two [sUrah]{.trn2}s in one [rakeah]{.trn2}.]{.trans}  


Other mental verbs,
like [ظَنَّ]{.ar}
usually require two direct objects.^[[شرح الرضي على الكافية (جامعة الإمام محمد)]{.ar} 2/988]
Even so,
sometimes they may take only one direct object
when that direct object refers to
the thought being perceived.
This is because, as we discussed in section () above, 
even when the mental verb takes two direct objects,
their [taqdIr]{.trn2} is a single direct object.^[[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 4/153](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1588&part=4#p-23090-1588-1)]
Here is an example of [ظَنَّ]{.ar} with one direct object:

(@) [وَلَقَدْ نَزَلْتِ فَلَا [تَظُنِّي غَيْرَهُ]{.eghl} مِنِّي بِمَنْزِلَةً الْمُحَبِّ الْمُكْرَمِ]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية (جامعة الإمام محمد)]{.ar} 2/988]{.citex}  
    [And surely you have alighted, so don't [assume other than it]{.eghl} from me, in the place of alighting of the honored beloved.]{.trans}  

[ظَنَّ]{.ar} in example () above has only one direct object [غَيْرَهُ]{.ar}.
Similarly, the single direct object of [ظَنَّ]{.ar}
can be a pronoun or pointing noun referring to the 
the thought being perceived.
For example:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ ذَاكَ]{.ar}
    [[[كتاب سيبويه]{.ar} 3/120](https://shamela.ws/book/23018/973)]{.citex}  
    [I thought that.]{.trans}  

In example () above,
[ذَاكَ]{.ar} can be the single direct object of [ظَنَّ]{.ar},
that refers to some thought.^[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} citing [الفراء]{.ar}]
The reason why [ذَاكَ]{.ar}
can be a direct object, and not necessarily refer to the [maSdar]{.trn2} as a absolute object
(as we will see shortly),
is because one can add the [maSdar]{.trn2} separately as the absolute object.
For example:

(@) [خِلْتُ ذَاكَ إِخَالُـ[ـهُ خَالًا]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[[شرح التسهيل لابن مالك]{.ar} 2/65](https://shamela.ws/book/13257/471)]{.citex}  
    [I imagined that, imagining [it [with] an imagining]{.eghl}.]{.trans}  
    ([خَالًا]{.ar} is the absolute object while [إِخَالُهُ]{.ar} is taking the pronoun [هُ]{.ar} as a direct object.)

Similarly, if someone says:

(@) [أَظُنُّ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [I assume Zayd to be standing.]{.trans}

then the reply to this can be:

(@) [أَنَا أَيْضًا أَظُنُّـ[ـهُ]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [I too assume [it]{.eghl}.]{.trans}  
    (The pronoun [هُ]{.ar} is a direct object and refers to the thought "Zayd is standing".)

Having said this,
some grammarians were of the opinion that
a single pronoun or pointing noun governed by [ظَنَّ]{.ar} can only
refer to the [maSdar]{.trn2} of [ظَنَّ]{.ar},
such that it is a deputy
to the [maSdar]{.trn2} as the absolute object.^[See [[التذييل والتكميل لأبي حيان]{.ar} 6/19](https://shamela.ws/book/17116/1710)]

[ظَنَّ]{.ar} can also occur with an indirect done-to,
which signifies the thing being thought _about_.
For example:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ [بِهِ]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 4/153](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1588&part=4#p-23090-1588-2)]{.citex}  
    [I thought [about him]{.eghl}.]{.trans}  


Consider also the following [Ayah]{.trn2}:

(@) [وَطَاۤىِٕفَةࣱ قَدۡ أَهَمَّتۡهُمۡ أَنفُسُهُمۡ [یَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ غَیۡرَ ٱلۡحَقِّ ظَنَّ ٱلۡجَـٰهِلِیَّةِۖ]{.eghl}]{.quran}  
    [[[سورة آل عمران]{.ar} 3:154](https://quran.com/3/154) cited by [[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 4/153](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1588&part=4#p-23090-1588-2)]{.citex}  
    [while another faction worried about themselves, thinking of Allāh other than the truth - the thought of ignorance]{.trans}

There are a few different analyses of [ظَنَّ]{.ar} and its
governees:

  i. [غَيْرَ الْحَقِّ]{.ar} is the direct object and [بِاللهِ]{.ar} is indicating who is being thought about,^[[[شرح الرضي على الكافية]{.ar} 4/153](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/23090/read?page=1588&part=4#p-23090-1588-2)] like:
     (@) [ظَنَنْتُ بِزَيْدٍ]{.ar}
         [[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة آل عمران]{.ar} 3:154](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/3/154)]{.citex}  
         [I thought about Zayd]{.trans}

 ii. [غَيْرَ الْحَقِّ]{.ar} is the first direct object and [بِاللهِ]{.ar} is the second direct object.^[[[التبيان في إعراب القرآن للعكبري]{.ar} 1/303](https://shamela.ws/book/22928/304)]
iii. [غَيْرَ الْحَقِّ]{.ar} is the a deputy to the [maSdar]{.trn2} as a absolute object, and [ظَنَّ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ]{.ar} is its substitute.^[[[الكشاف للزمخشري]{.ar} for [سورة آل عمران]{.ar} 3:154](https://tafsir.app/kashaf/3/154)]

## Suppressing one or both direct objects

Non-mental verbs
that can take two direct objects
may sometimes take
only one direct object.
So, for example, instead of saying:

(@) [أَعْطَيْتُ زَيْدًا دِرْهَمًا]{.ar}  
    [I gave Zayd a dirham.]{.trans}

we can say both:

(@) [أَعْطَيْتُ دِرْهَمًا]{.ar}  
    [[Howell §443 2/152](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=213)]{.citex}  
    [I gave a dirham.]{.trans}

(@) [أَعْطَيْتُ زَيْدًا]{.ar}  
    [[Howell §443 2/152](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=213)]{.citex}  
    [I gave Zayd.]{.trans}

Mental verbs,
on the other hand,
generally need both direct objects.
So, for example, instead of saying:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §443 2/154](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=215)]{.citex}  
    [I thought Zayd to be standing.]{.trans}

we cannot say (without context):

(@) ✗ [ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §443 2/154](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=215)]{.citex}

(@) ✗ [ظَنَنْتُ قَائِمًا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §443 2/154](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=215)]{.citex}

However, it is possible to omit one of the two direct objects
if its meaning is implied and is indicated by context.^[[Howell §443 2/153](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=214)]
For example,

(@) [وَلَا [یَحۡسَبَنَّ]{.eghl} ٱلَّذِینَ یَبۡخَلُونَ بِمَاۤ ءَاتَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضۡلِهِۦ [هُوَ خَیۡرࣰا لَّهُمۖ]{.eghl}]{.quran}
    [[[سورة آل عمران]{.ar} 3:180](https://quran.com/3/180) cited by [Howell §443 2/153--154](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=214)^[cited as III. 175]]{.citex}  
    [And let not those who [greedily] withhold what Allāh has given them of His bounty [ever think that it is better for them]{.eghl}.]{.trans}

In the [Ayah]{.trn2} above,
the first direct object of
[يَحْسَبَنَّ]{.ar}
is interpreted
(in one interpretation of this reading)
to be a suppressed [بُخْلَهُمْ]{.ar}
[their miserliness]{.trans},
and [هُوَ]{.ar} is a separating-pronoun.
Such that the meaning is:

(@) [ولا يَحْسَبَنَّ الباخِلون [بُخْلَهم]{.eghl} هو خيرًا لهم]{.ar}
    [[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة آل عمران]{.ar} 3:180](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/3/180)]{.citex}  
    [And let not the misers think [their miserliness]{.eghl} to be good for them.]{.trans}

Both direct objects can also be omitted together.
For example:

<!--
(@) [وَظَنَنتُمۡ ظَنَّ ٱلسَّوۡءِ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الفتح]{.ar} 48:12](https://quran.com/48/12) cited by [Howell §443 2/153](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=214)]{.citex}  
    [And you assumed an assumption of evil]{.trans}  
    ([ظَنَّ]{.ar} is analyzed to be a absolute object.^[[[إعراب القرآن للدرويش]{.ar} for [سورة الفتح]{.ar} 48:12](https://tafsir.app/iraab-aldarweesh/48/12)])  

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ ذَاكَ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §443 2/154](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=215)]{.citex}  
    [I thought that.]{.trans}  
    ([ذَاكَ]{.ar} is a deputy to the [maSdar]{.trn2} as the absolute object.^[But see also [[التذييل والتكميل لأبي حيان]{.ar} 6/19](https://shamela.ws/book/17116/1710)])
-->

(@) [مَنْ يَسْمَعْ يَخَلْ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §443 2/153](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=214)]{.citex}  
    [Whoso hears, will think.]{.trans}  

The preposition [بِ]{.ar} may be used with [ظَنَّ]{.ar} to mean [about]{.trans}.
In this case as well, no direct object is needed.
For example:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ بِهِ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §443 2/154](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=215)]{.citex}  
    [I thought about him.]{.trans}

Even in such cases where both direct objects are omitted,
their meaning may be implied.
For example:

(@) [وَیَوۡمَ یُنَادِیهِمۡ فَیَقُولُ أَیۡنَ شُرَكَاۤءِیَ ٱلَّذِینَ [كُنتُمۡ تَزۡعُمُونَ]{.eghl}]{.quran}
    [[[سورة القصص]{.ar} 28:62](https://quran.com/28/62) cited by [Howell §443 2/153](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=214)]{.citex}  
    [And [warn of] the Day He will call them and say, "Where are My 'partners' which [you used to claim]{.eghl}?"]{.trans}  

In the [Ayah]{.trn2} above, the two suppressed direct objects of [تَزْعُمُونَ]{.ar}
are interpreted to be thus:

(@) [تَزْعُمُونَهُمْ شُرَكَاءَ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §443 2/153](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=214)]{.citex}  
    [...\ you claim them to be partners]{.trans}

Suppressing one or both direct objects in the answer to a question is especially common.
For example, in response to the question:

(@) [أتظن زيدًا قائما]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للشاطبي]{.ar} 2/495](https://shamela.ws/book/20562/1156)]{.citex}  
    [Do you think Zayd to be standing?]{.trans}

All three of the following replies are acceptable:

(@) [ظننت زيدًا]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للشاطبي]{.ar} 2/495](https://shamela.ws/book/20562/1156)]{.citex}  
    [I think Zayd [to be standing].]{.trans}

(@) [ظننتُ قائمًا]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للشاطبي]{.ar} 2/495](https://shamela.ws/book/20562/1156)]{.citex}  
    [I think [Zayd to be] standing.]{.trans}

(@) [ظننت]{.ar}
    [[[شرح ألفية ابن مالك للشاطبي]{.ar} 2/495](https://shamela.ws/book/20562/1156)]{.citex}  
    [I think [Zayd to be standing].]{.trans}

Similarly:

(@) [قُلْتُ صَلَّاهَا النَّبِيُّ ﷺ  قَالَ لَا إِخَالُ]{.ar}
    [[[مصنف ابن أبي شيبة]{.ar} :7856](https://hadithunlocked.com/ibnabishaybah:7856)]{.citex}  
    [I said, "Did the Prophet [ﷺ]{.areng} pray it?" He said, "I don't think so."]{.trans}  

## Suspension of government {#sec-ta3leeq}

Sometimes,
there can be a sentence where a
mental verb
does not take its direct object(s)
directly.
Instead its
direct government
is _suspended_ due to the presence of a _suspender_.
This phenomenon is called
_suspension_ of government.
Let's take a look at an example.
Consider a sentence where [ظَنَّ]{.ar} exercises it governing effect.

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا قَائِمًا]{.ar}
    [I thought Zayd to be standing.]{.trans}  

Now let's see what happens when the
original
subject
([زَيْد]{.ar})
and info
([قَائِم]{.ar})
are preceded by a [لَ]{.ar} of beginning.
The sentence becomes:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ لَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/158](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=219)]{.citex}  
    [I thought, assuredly Zayd is standing.]{.trans}  

As you can see,
the
original
subject
([زَيْد]{.ar})
and info
([قَائِم]{.ar})
are now both in the u-case.
This is because the effect of the [لَ]{.ar} of beginning
is to cause a
subject
and info
to be in the u-case.
The government of [ظَنَّ]{.ar} is thus suspended.
The inner sentence
[لَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}
is said to be in the positional a-case
as a direct object of [ظَنَّ]{.ar} that fulfils the role of two direct objects.

The proof that the inner sentence
[لَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}
is in the positional a-case
and that the government of [ظَنَّ]{.ar} is suspended,
is that if we were to put a conjunction after this sentence,
then the governing effect of [ظَنَّ]{.ar} would resume.
For example:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ لَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ [وَعَمْرًا مُنْطَلِقًا]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/158](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=219)]{.citex}  
    [I thought, assuredly Zayd is standing [and [#eamr]{.trn2} is setting out]{.eghl}.]{.trans}  

The suspenders that suspend the government of
the mental verbs are discussed in the subsections below:

### The negaters [مَا]{.ar}, [إِنْ]{.ar}, and [لَا]{.ar}

Examples:

(@) [لَقَدۡ عَلِمۡتَ مَا هَـٰۤؤُلَاۤءِ یَنطِقُونَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأنبياء]{.ar} 21:65](https://quran.com/21/65) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/346; [Howell §445 2/160](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=221)]{.citex}  
    ["You have already known that these do not speak!"]{.trans}  

In example () above, the negater [مَا]{.ar} prevents [عَلِمْتَ]{.ar} from
directly governing two direct objects. Instead,
the sentence
[مَا هَؤُلَاءِ يَنْطِقُونَ]{.ar}
is in the positional a-case as a direct object
that fulfils the role two direct objects.
Similarly:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ وَاللهِ إِنْ زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/160](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=221)]{.citex}  
    [I knew, by Allāh, Zayd is not standing.]{.trans}  

(@) [یَوۡمَ یَدۡعُوكُمۡ فَتَسۡتَجِیبُونَ بِحَمۡدِهِۦ وَتَظُنُّونَ إِن لَّبِثۡتُمۡ إِلَّا قَلِیلࣰا]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الإسراء]{.ar} 17:52](https://quran.com/17/52) cited by [Howell §445 2/160](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=221)]{.citex}  
    [On the Day He will call you and you will respond with praise of Him and think that you had not remained [in the world] except for a little."]{.trans}  

(@) [عَلِمْتُ وَاللهِ لَا زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ ولَا عَمْرٌو]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/160](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=221)]{.citex}  
    [I knew, by Allāh, Zayd is not in the house, nor [#eamr]{.trn2}.]{.trans}  


### [لَ]{.ar} of beginning

We have already seen in example () above, how [لَ]{.ar} of beginning suspends
the direct government of a mental verb.
Here is another example:

(@) [وَلَقَدۡ [عَلِمُوا۟ لَمَنِ]{.eghl} ٱشۡتَرَىٰهُ مَا لَهُۥ فِی ٱلۡـَٔاخِرَةِ مِنۡ خَلَـٰقࣲۚ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة البقرة]{.ar} 2:102](https://quran.com/2/102) cited by [Howell §445 2/160](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=221)]{.citex}  
    [But [they [i.e., the Children of Israel] certainly knew that whoever]{.eghl} purchased it [i.e., magic] would not have in the Hereafter any share.]{.trans}  


### [لَ]{.ar} of oath

(@) [لَقدْ عَلِمْتُ لَتَأْتِيَنَّ مَنِيَّتِي ~ إِنَّ الْمَنَايًا لَا تَطِيشُ سِهَامُهَا]{.ar}
    [[النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/346; [Howell §445 2/158](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=219)]{.citex}  
    [And assuredly, I have known (by God) verily my fate will come. Verily the fates---their arrows do not miss.]{.trans}  

The presence of the [لَ]{.ar} of oath in 
[لَتَأْتِيَنَّ]{.ar}
suspends the direct government of [عَلِمْتُ]{.ar}.
Otherwise the sentence would have been:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ مَنِيَّتِي آتِيَةً]{.ar}
    [[النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/436]{.citex}  
    [I have known my fate to be coming.]{.trans}  

### A question sentence

A question sentence can follow
a mental verb
and in such a case
the government of the mental verb
is suspended
if the entire question sentence
is its direct object.

Here is an example:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ أَزَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ أَمْ عَمْرٌو]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/159](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=220)]{.citex}  
    [I knew whether Zayd was in the house or [#eamr]{.trn2}.]{.trans}  

In example () above,
the entire question sentence
[أَزَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ أَمْ عَمْرٌو]{.ar}
is in the a-case
and it fulfils the role the two direct objects of [عَلِمْتُ]{.ar}.
That is the traditional explanation.
However, it is also possible that
[عَلِمَ]{.ar} here requires only one direct object.
In which case the question sentence
fulfils the role the one required direct object.

Another point to note is that the question sentence
is now no longer a question to the listener.
That is why we have not puntuated the translation with a question mark (?).
Rather, the entire example sentence
is signifying that the speaker knows the answer to the question.

Here is another example:

(@) [وَلَتَعۡلَمُنَّ أَیُّنَاۤ أَشَدُّ عَذَابࣰا وَأَبۡقَىٰ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة طه]{.ar} 20:71](https://quran.com/20/71) cited by [Howell §445 2/159](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=220)]{.citex}  
    [and you will surely know which of us is more severe in [giving] punishment and more enduring]{.trans}

In example () above,
there are three possible interpretations^[[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة طه]{.ar} 20:71](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/20/71)]:

a. The first interpretation, and the one relevant to our discussion here,
   is that [أَيّ]{.ar} is a subject and [أَشَدّ]{.ar} is its info.
   The question sentence
   [أَیُّنَا أَشَدُّ عَذَابًا وَأَبْقَىٰ]{.ar}
   fulfils the role the two direct objects of [تَعْلَمُنَّ]{.ar}.
b. Another interpretation is [تَعْلَمُنَّ]{.ar} here only requires one direct object
   and the question sentence is that (positional) direct object.
c. A third interpretation is that [أَيّ]{.ar} is a connected noun.
   [أَيّ]{.ar} itself (not the entire question sentence) is the direct object of
   [تَعْلَمُنَّ]{.ar}.
   And [أَيّ]{.ar} is inflexible ending with a [Dammah]{.trn2} because of a phenomenon described in @sec-mabny_ayy.

Here are some more examples:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ مَتَىٰ السَّفَرُ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/159](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=220)]{.citex}  
    [I knew when the journey was (or would be).]{.trans}

(@) [عَلِمْتُ أَبُو مَنْ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/159](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=220)]{.citex}  
    [I knew whose father was Zayd.]{.trans}

(@) [عَلِمْتُ صَبِيحَةَ أَيِّ يَوْمٍ سَفَرُكَ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/159](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=220)]{.citex}  
    [I knew the morning of which day your journey was (or will be).]{.trans}

(@) [وَسَیَعۡلَمُ ٱلَّذِینَ ظَلَمُوۤا۟ أَیَّ مُنقَلَبࣲ یَنقَلِبُونَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الشعراء]{.ar} 26:227](https://quran.com/26/227) cited by [Howell §445 2/159](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=220)]{.citex}  
    [And those who have wronged are going to know to what [kind of] return they will be returned.]{.trans}  

In example () above, [أَيّ]{.ar} is a question-device in the a-case as a absolute object, governed by [يَنْقَلِبُونَ]{.ar}.^[[[الدر المصون للسمين الحلبي]{.ar} for [سورة الشعراء]{.ar} 26:227](https://tafsir.app/aldur-almasoon/26/227)]
The entire question sentence is in the a-case governed by [سَيَعْلَمُ]{.ar}.

### Other suspenders of government

There are other, less common, suspenders
discussed by the grammarians.
We will list some of them below:

#### [لَعَلَّ]{.ar} {.unnumbered}

Example:

(@) [وَإِنۡ أَدۡرِی [لَعَلَّهُۥ]{.eghl} فِتۡنَةࣱ لَّكُمۡ وَمَتَـٰعٌ إِلَىٰ حِینࣲ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأنبياء]{.ar} 21:111](https://quran.com/21/111) cited by [Howell §445 2/160](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=221)]{.citex}  
    [And I know not; [perhaps]{.eghl} it is a trial for you and enjoyment for a time."]{.trans}  

#### The conditional-device [لَوْ]{.ar} {.unnumbered}

For example:

(@) [وَلَقَدْ عَلِمَ الْأَقْوَامُ [لَوْ]{.eghl} أَنَّ حَاتِمًا ~ أَرَادَ ثَرَاءَ الْمَالِ كَانَ لَهُ وَفْرٌ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/160](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=221)]{.citex}  
    [And the peoples have known that had [#HAtim]{.trn2} desired abundance of property, he would have had affluence.]{.trans}  

#### [إِنَّ]{.ar} that has a differentiator [لَ]{.ar}

Example:

(@) [عَلِمْتُ إِنَّ زَيْدًا لَقَائِمٌ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/161](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=222)]{.citex}  
    [I knew: indeed Zayd is standing.]{.trans}  

### The verbs whose government may be suspended

Suspension of government is possible for the following categories of verbs:

#### The flexible mental verbs that take two direct objects {.unnumbered}

We have seen examples of suspension with mental verbs that take two direct objects like [ظَنَّ]{.ar}, [عَلِمَ]{.ar}, [حَسِبَ]{.ar}, etc.
above.

mental verbs that are rigid
like
[هَبْ]{.ar} [grant]{.trans}
and
[تَعَلَّمْ]{.ar} [learn]{.trans},
which are only used in the verb of command,
are excluded from having their government suspended.

The verbs of rendering,
like
[صَيَّرَ]{.ar} [to make _x_ become _y_]{.trans}
[تَرَكَ]{.ar} [to leave _x_ as _y_]{.trans},
etc.,
are also excluded.

#### Any other mental verb even if it does not take two direct objects {.unnumbered}

Some mental verbs may take only one direct object, like
[عَرَفَ]{.ar} [to recognize, know]{.trans}.
These too are subject to suspension.
So, for example, we can say:

(@) [عَرَفْتُ مَنْ أَبُوكَ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/164](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=225)]{.citex}  
    [I knew who your father is/was.]{.trans}  

In example () above,
[عَرَفْتُ]{.ar} would have taken a noun as a direct object,
but the question-device suspends its government
and so the entire question sentence
[مَنْ أَبُوكَ]{.ar}
fulfils the role of its direct object.

Other mental verbs that take only only one direct object
(like [عَلِمَ]{.ar} when used to mean [to know]{.trans}),
or that take an indirect direct object 
(like [تَفَكَّرَ فِي]{.ar} [to think about]{.trans}),
are also similarly subject to suspension.^[[Howell §445 2/164](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=225)]

#### Verbs which can enable the mental verbs {.unnumbered}

There are some verbs that are not mental verbs per se,
but they can enable
the mental verbs.
These verbs too may be subject to suspension.^[[[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 446](https://archive.org/details/0969pdf_201912/page/n445/mode/2up)]
Let's explain what we mean with some examples.

<!--
The verb
[سَمِعَ]{.ar}
[to hear]{.trans}
is a sensory verb, not a mental verb.
But hearing enables one to _know_.
[سَمِعَ]{.ar}
can even take two direct objects, for example:

(@) [سَمِعْتُ زَيْدٌ قَارِئًا]{.ar}
    [[[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 446](https://archive.org/details/0969pdf_201912/page/n445/mode/1up)]{.citex}  
    [I heard Zayd reading.]{.trans}  

(@) [سَمِعْتُ زَيْدٌ يَقْرَأُ]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/165](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=226)]{.citex}  
    [I heard Zayd reading.]{.trans}  
-->

The verb [رَأَى]{.ar} [to see]{.trans}
enables its doer to _know_.
Therefore, it may be subject to suspension of government.
For example:

(@) [أَمَا تَرَى أَيُّ بَرْقٍ هَـٰهُنَا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §445 2/165](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=226)]{.citex}  
    [Do you not see which [kind of] lightning is here?]{.trans}  

Similarly,
the verb [سَأَلَ]{.ar}
[to ask]{.trans}
enables one to know.
Therefore its government can be suspended.
For example:

(@) [اسْأَلْ أَيُّهُمْ زَيْدٌ]{.ar}
    [[[البسيط لابن أبي الربيع]{.ar} 446](https://archive.org/details/0969pdf_201912/page/n445/mode/1up)]{.citex}  
    [Ask which of them is Zayd]{.trans}

(@) [یَسۡـَٔلُونَ أَیَّانَ یَوۡمُ ٱلدِّینِ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الذاريات]{.ar} 51:12](https://quran.com/51/12) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/347]{.citex}  
    [They ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"]{.trans}  

The same can be said of the verb
[نَظَرَ]{.ar} [to look]{.trans}.
Example:

(@) [فَلۡیَنظُرۡ أَیُّهَاۤ أَزۡكَىٰ طَعَامࣰا]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الكهف]{.ar} 18:19](https://quran.com/18/19) cited by [النحو العربي: أحكام ومعان]{.ar} 1/347]{.citex}  
    [and let him look to which is the best of food]{.trans}  
   
## Neutralization of government

Similar to suspension is
is another phenomenon called _neutralization_.
Neutralization
occurs when a mental verb exercises no government at all.

Consider the following sentence:

(@) [ظَنَنْتُ زَيْدًا عَالِمًا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §444 2/155](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=216)]{.citex}  
    [I thought Zayd to be knowledgeable.]{.trans}  

In example () above,
[ظَنَّ]{.ar} is governing
the original subject ([زَيْد]{.ar})
and original info ([عَالِم]{.ar})
as usual.

If we move the position of the verb
(as is allowed),
then the 
the original subject ([زَيْد]{.ar})
and original info ([عَالِم]{.ar})
can remain direct objects.
So we can say:

(@) [زَيْدًا [ظَنَنْتُ]{.eghl} عَالِمًا]{.ar}
    [[Howell §444 2/155](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=216)]{.citex}  
    [Zayd [I thought]{.eghl} to be knowledgeable.]{.trans}  

(@) [زَيْدًا عَالِمً [اظَنَنْتُ]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[Howell §444 2/155](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=216)]{.citex}  
    [Zayd to be knowledgeable [I thought]{.eghl}.]{.trans}  

However, 
when the verb is moved from its initial position to an intervening or final position,
then its government may optionally be _neutralized_.
In that case,
[زَيْد]{.ar}
and
[عَالِم]{.ar}
stay as
the subject
and info,
in the u-case.
So we can say:

(@) [زَيْدٌ [ظَنَنْتُ]{.eghl} عَالِمٌ]{.ar}
    [Zayd [I thought]{.eghl} to be knowledgeable.]{.trans}  

(@) [زَيْدٌ عَالِمٌ [اظَنَنْتُ]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[Howell §444 2/156](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=217)]{.citex}  
    [Zayd to be knowledgeable [I thought]{.eghl}.]{.trans}  


The difference between
neutralization
and
suspension
is that
suspension
still governs in meaning, if not in wording.
It's just that the suspender
introduces a new sentence that then fulfils the role the
direct objects of the mental verb.
Whereas, in the case of neutralization,
there is no government of the mental verb
whether in meaning or in wording.

The standard rule is that neutralization is only allowed
when the verb is in an intervening or final position,
as in examples () and () above.

When the verb is in an intervening position,
then both government (example ())
and neutralization (example ())
are equally permissible.
And when the verb is in the final position,
then neutralization (example ()) is considered better,
while government (example ()) is also permissible.^[[Howell §444 2/156](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=217)]

When the verb is in the initial position,
as in example () above,
then,
as we have already mentioned,
the standard rule is that
neutralization is disallowed.^[[Howell §444 2/156](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=217)]
So the verb must govern the
the original subject
and original info
as direct objects.

However,
there are instances of a verb occurring in initial position while the
the original subject
and original info
remain in the u-case.
These are then explained away using [taqdIr]{.trn2}.
For example:

(@) [أَرْجُو وَآمُلُ أَنْ بَدْنُو مَوَدَّتُهَا * وَمَا [إِخَالُ لَدَيْنَا مِنْكَ تَنْوِيلُ]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[Howell §444 2/156](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=217)]{.citex}  
    [I hope and faintly expect that her love may approach; but I fancy not a bestowal of favor from you to us.]{.trans}  

In example () above [تَنْوِيلُ]{.ar} is in the u-case
while [إِخَالُ]{.ar} precedes it.
To reconcile this,
a deleted state-of-affairs pronoun is [taqdIr]{.trn2}ed as the first direct object of [إِخَالُ]{.ar}.
The second (positional) direct object is then the following sentence.
The complete [taqdIr]{.trn2} is:

(@) [إِخَالُـ[ـهُ]{.eghl} لَدَيْنَا مِنْكَ تَنْوِيلُ]{.ar}

Similarly:

(@) [كَذَاكَ أُدِّبْتُ حَتَّى صَارَ مِنْ خُلُقِي * أَنِّي [وَجَدْتُ مِلَاكُ الشِّيمَةِ الْأَدَبُ]{.eghl}]{.ar}
    [[Howell §444 2/157](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=218)]{.citex}  
    [Thus was I trained to good behavior until it became [a part] of my nature, that I perceived the basis of character to be training.]{.trans}  

In example () above,
[مِلَاكُ]{.ar}
are
[الْأَدَبُ]{.ar}
are in the u-case,
even though the verb [وَجَدْتُ]{.ar} precedes them.
To reconcile this,
a deleted [لَ]{.ar} of beginning is [taqdIr]{.trn2}ed, 
suspending the government of [وَجَدْتُ]{.ar}, thus:

(@) [وَجَدْتُ [لَـ]{.eghl}ـمِلَاكُ الشِّيمَةِ الْأَدَبُ]{.ar}

Some grammarians allowed neutralization even when the verb is in the initial position.
They then do not require [taqdIr]{.trn2} to explain the above verses.^[[Howell §444 2/157](https://adamiturabi.github.io/howell-navigator/content/2-07-0.html?page=218)]
